Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed cross-sectional secondary biomarker analysis•July 1, 2026

PET, CSF, and plasma discordance was modeled as probability, not test error

In 320 ADNI participants, PET and CSF classifications disagreed in 12% even when obtained within seven days; a latent-class model used plasma Aβ42/40 or %p-tau217 to refine uncertainty rather than declaring either PET or CSF an infallible reference.

Key quantitative results: PET-CSF discordance occurred in 12 of 98 participants tested within seven days (12%; 95% CI, 7%-20%).

BiomarkersBloodAmyloidAβ42/Aβ40Biological confirmation

Added October 14, 2026 · DOI:10.1038/s44400-026-00109-4

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Diagnostic accuracy depends on what is treated as truth. The analysis found clinically meaningful PET-CSF disagreement even with close timing and showed how plasma can refine, but not erase, uncertainty. Sparse discordant cells and model assumptions limit direct clinical use.

Study design

Cross-sectional secondary analysis of one prespecified PET-anchored PET-CSF-plasma triad per ADNI participant (n=320). Bayesian latent-class models estimated amyloid probability from PET, CSF, and plasma Aβ42/40 or %p-tau217, with sensitivity analyses for timing, CSF cutoffs, and PET-CSF conditional dependence.

Key quantitative results

  • PET-CSF discordance occurred in 12 of 98 participants tested within seven days (12%; 95% CI, 7%-20%).
  • Concordant PET-positive/CSF-positive and PET-negative/CSF-negative patterns mapped to posterior probabilities near 1 and 0, respectively.
  • Discordant patterns produced intermediate, often wide probabilities that shifted with plasma strata and dependence assumptions.
  • The primary Elecsys CSF Aβ42/40 analysis was available in 138 of 320 participants, and several discordant three-test cells were sparse or unobserved.

What changed

The paper reframed multi-modality disagreement as an explicit uncertainty problem and demonstrated a way to avoid forcing every discordant result into a false-positive or false-negative label.

Strength of evidence

Exploratory methodological evidence using a well-characterized research cohort and prespecified sensitivity analyses. Clinical transportability is limited by selected ADNI participants, incomplete CSF-ratio data, sparse discordant patterns, and model assumptions.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

When PET, CSF, and plasma disagree, interpretation should consider biology, timing, cutoffs, prevalence, and uncertainty rather than assuming a single modality is always correct.

Field medical relevance

Useful for questions about discordant blood, CSF, and PET results; comparator choice in validation studies; and the limits of single-reference sensitivity and specificity claims.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The work highlights reference-standard dependence: apparent blood-test errors can reflect PET-CSF biological or threshold discordance. It supports reporting uncertainty around discordant patterns rather than oversimplifying one comparator as ground truth.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The framework could eventually reduce unnecessary repeat testing in discordant cases, but it did not evaluate utilization, costs, coverage, or access.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does plasma resolve every PET-CSF disagreement?
No. It refined probabilities, but discordant patterns remained uncertain and some cells had very small samples.
Is PET the gold standard in this model?
No. PET, CSF, and plasma were treated as imperfect indicators of a latent amyloid state.
Can the posterior probabilities be used clinically now?
No. The authors framed this as an interpretive research approach, not a validated routine-care decision tool.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • ADNI research cohort
  • Only 138 participants had the primary CSF Aβ42/40 measure
  • Sparse discordant pattern cells
  • Dependence and identifiability assumptions
  • No prospective clinical utility evaluation

Primary source · DOI

Verma K, Kumar S. Amyloid probability in Alzheimer disease from plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, and amyloid imaging. npj Dement. 2026;2:49. doi:10.1038/s44400-026-00109-4.
